items.title: Ukraine confirms it sank Russian corvette in Libyan port
items.summary:
GLASGOW, Scotland — Ukraine was behind the explosive sinking of the Russian corvette Merkury in the Libyan port of Benghazi over the weekend, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, and the country’s military released accompanying videos. 

The Merkury, a warship that had been acquired by the Russian navy in 2023, was left mostly submerged after sea drones struck it on Nov. 22. The video released by Ukrainian authorities shows several of the uncrewed, explosive-laden boats slamming into the side of the moored ship. 

The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) says it carried out the operation jointly with Ukraine’s Defense Forces. Zelenskyy said seven Ukrainian-made naval drones were used in the operation and that a Ka-27 helicopter aboard the corvette was also destroyed.

During the same operation, the Russian dry-cargo ship MV Angara was also targeted. The SBU describes Angara as a sanctioned vessel used to move weapons and military equipment on Russian routes to Syria and Libya, and says Merkury had escorted it.

items.title: Canada joins NATO innovation fund, promises ‘business as usual’ with US

It was a calm reply about an extraordinary development between formerly close allies, but in one sense, it was quite true. As the Trump administration reduces its contributions to the alliance—and in some cases threatens military action against its members—they are increasing their efforts to build their own militaries and industry.

The Canadian decision pushes total commitments to the NATO Innovation Fund past 1.1 billion euros. Joining the fund also makes Canadian defense startups eligible to draw upon it, giving them another source of capital and access to the fund’s network of venture capitalists.

items.title: The military lacks an ‘overarching plan’ to improve munition stockpiles—partly because it’s no one’s job
items.summary:
The Defense Department has no “overarching plan” to identify, achieve, or measure its progress toward long-term munition production goals, according to a Government Accountability Office study released on Thursday, which said the military was too reactive to global events and unprepared to forecast its own needs.

The GAO cited—among other issues—a lack of centralized authority over weapons inventories, which have been depleted by the Iran war and are vital to U.S. plans for a potential conflict with China.

At the center of the problem lies a discrepancy between what the military can buy and what it actually needs, which the GAO said could even result in munition investments that exceed the Pentagon’s requirements. 

“While DOD is taking steps to focus on munitions shortages, it is not positioned to address these gaps,” the report’s authors wrote. “DOD does not have an overarching plan or designated and empowered leadership to improve munition inventories and meet its munitions requirements. By not identifying long-term goals, strategies to achieve them, and metrics to gauge progress, DOD cannot be sure that its actions will address its munition shortfalls. ”

The Naval Criminal Investigative Service, which handles the Navy’s felony-level probes, is investigating retired Marine Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal , Military Times confirmed Friday. CBS News was first to report on the investigation.

A Marine Corps spokesperson told Military Times that the service is aware of the allegations against Kasal, which occurred while he worked as a civilian JROTC instructor at the Basic Academy of International Studies in Henderson, Nevada.

Although the Corps did not specify the time frame of the investigation, Kasal was employed by the Clark County School District three months after his retirement from the Corps in August 2018. He later resigned in August 2025, the school district told CBS.

The school district did not immediately return a Military Times request for comment.

The service’s and NCIS’ spokesperson both said no further details are to be released at this time to “protect the integrity of the investigation.”

items.title: Trump, Dana White donate $500,000 to Marine Corps band members
items.summary:
President Donald Trump and Ultimate Fighting Championship President and CEO Dana White announced on Friday they would make a combined personal donation of $500,000 to the U.S. Marine Corps band.

Trump first announced the intention at a White House press briefing, calling it a “big award” to be split among the 135 members of the band, known as “The President’s Own.”

Previously, Trump and White were expected to donate a total of $200,000 —$100,000 each — but at a Friday afternoon White House reception, the president announced their contribution would instead be more than doubled to $500,000 to accommodate the number of individuals in the band. Trump said he initially thought there were only around 70 members.

“Dana and I are contributing the $500,000 to express our immense appreciation for your spectacular talent, unwavering professionalism, which it is, and total commitment to excellence in everything that you’ve done, and that includes those people that make it possible for you to play so well,” Trump said during the reception. 

The increase from $200,000 to $500,000 boosted the bonus amount for each band member from around $1,481 to roughly $3,703. The band’s website features musicians, as well as stage crew, communication specialists and other roles.

It’s entirely a personal donation, and no taxpayer dollars are being used, a White House official confirmed to Military Times.

items.t: Trump, Dana White donate $500,000 to Marine Corps band members

The Karpat (meaning Carpathians, after the mountain range) made its first public dynamic appearance yesterday at Slovakia’s Záhorie Military Testing Area, demonstrating its mobility off-road and firing its main gun. items.title: Senator moves to strip controversial cuts from sweeping veterans benefits bill
items.summary:
The chairman of the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee proposed changes Friday to a sweeping veterans benefits bill that would eliminate proposed fee increases on VA home loans and revise disability compensation provisions opposed by several veterans organizations .

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan. , proposed a substitute amendment to the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act , which passed the House on Veterans Day and awaits Senate action.

The House-passed bill would raise fees for certain VA home loan refinancing transactions from 0.5% to 1.42% and double mortgage assumption fees from 0.5% to 1%. Moran’s amendment would eliminate both increases. 

The amendment would also alter the bill’s changes to disability compensation for tinnitus, preserving standalone tinnitus ratings, according to a summary of Moran’s proposal.

The House proposal would eliminate separate compensable ratings for tinnitus, or ringing in the ears, while retaining a 10% rating in a specified circumstance involving service-connected hearing loss.

Moran’s office told Military Times that his amendment would allow veterans to establish service connection for tinnitus on its own. VA would generally assign a 0% rating — which carries no monthly disability payment — for tinnitus alone. 

Moran’s office said a 0% rating could provide a path to VA healthcare enrollment and allow veterans to file claims for secondary conditions they can show were caused by tinnitus, such as migraines or mental health conditions. The office said VA’s 2022 proposed rule would have eliminated tinnitus as a standalone rating…
items.t: Senator moves to strip controversial cuts from sweeping veterans benefits bill

items.title: Navy’s 2027 shipbuilding plan would cost $54B a year, federal agency says
items.summary:
The Congressional Budget Office released a report Thursday breaking down the financial implications of the U.S. Navy’s 2027 plan to invest in more ships and unmanned vessels over the next 30 years.

The federal agency predicted that the annual cost of building ships will hover around $54 billion in 2026 dollars, an 18% uptick from the Navy’s analysis, according to the office.

“CBO estimates that the Navy’s 2027 plan would cost 41 percent more annually in real terms (that is, with costs adjusted to remove the effects of inflation) than the average amount appropriated over the past 5 years,” the report said.

As part of its shipbuilding blueprint, the Navy would increase the number of ships in the fleet from 286 to 398 by 2056; purchase 371 new combat ships and combat logistics and support ships; 58 new and 29 used auxiliary ships; 72 medium unmanned surface vessels; and 15 nuclear-powered guided missile battleships.

But maintenance delays that have plagued the Navy for over a decade would still prevent the Navy from wielding the full offensive capabilities of the vessels if not addressed, the report said.

Extended deployments of ships like the USS Abraham Lincoln, USS Gerald R. Ford and USS Spruance during the Iran war impact vital maintenance availability windows for those ships, prolonging the amount of time before they are deployable again.

The CBO quantified that just building new ships would cost an average of $48.9 billion a year, whereas the Navy assessed that construction would cost $41.1 billion.

items.title: Army delays detonation of unstable ammunition stockpile until Monday
items.summary:
The Army has delayed the controversial detonation of an unstable ammunition stockpile stored at an Iowa munitions facility until Monday, the acting secretary of the Army confirmed, following a barrage of complaints from officials and communities in the projected path of its blast plume. 

Citing public safety and communication, Adam Telle said he had directed officials to postpone the blasts — originally planned for Friday — until Monday, just three days later. 

“This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material,” he said in a Thursday statement posted to social media. The Army fears that dropping Iowa temperatures could cause an inadvertent explosion. 

“The primary concern that we have right now is that lead azide can become more volatile when it is exposed to lower temperatures, and as the weather in Iowa gets colder, we’re very concerned that there could be uncontrolled detonation,” Army spokeswoman Justine Barati told Iowa Public Radio .

The controlled demolition, originally planned for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, is intended to dispose of more than 9,000 pounds of degraded lead azide, an extremely sensitive compound the military often uses in blasting caps and detonators. The plant, located near Burlington, makes medium- and large-caliber ammunition for the Department of Defense. 

Lead is a highly toxic substance that is especially dangerous for young children and pregnant people, as it can affect brain development and cause permanent health…
items.t: Army delays detonation of unstable ammunition stockpile until Monday

items.title: Trump, Xi agreed that military AI decisions should involve humans, Bessent says
items.summary:
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed humans should always be involved in military decisions that use artificial intelligence technologies, even as the two countries compete for AI supremacy , Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday.

Bessent told CNBC after returning from Trump’s meeting with Xi in Shenzhen, China, that the agreement was among the major achievements of Trump’s trip to Asia.

“I think it was very important that President Trump and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions,” Bessent said, referring to the Trump administration’s preferred term for the technology, “super intelligence.”

Bessent said that the U.S.-China agreement on military use of the technology, requiring human involvement and other safeguards, would not be affected by the two countries’ competition for AI supremacy. He added that U.S. AI labs needed to maintain their technological lead as the best defense against “dangerous” Chinese AI models that are being used in cyberattacks.

“But there’s nothing to do with competition when it says that both sides agree that no major military operation should be launched without a human being involved,” Bessent said.

Tuesday’s operation took out the road bridge span but left the rail span still standing. Amazingly trains were still running despite the remaining side being pummeled by weapons over two nights and clearly damaged. Dropping the rail portion would sever the vital conduit between Crimea and Russia entirely.

Video from a Russian passenger train passing the section of the Kerch Bridge road span that was destroyed by Ukrainian drones/missiles. pic.twitter.com/NypzkoD0Of 

— Mike Eckel (@Mike_Eckel) November 18, 2026 

“As a result of another attack on the Crimean Bridge, traffic has been temporarily suspended,” Aksyonov stated on Telegram , using the Russian term for the bridge. “All relevant services are on duty. An assessment of the damage is underway. Further information will be provided as it becomes available.”

So far, Ukrainian authorities haven’t commented on the attack. We have reached out to President Volodymyr Zelensky’s office, the Security Service of Ukraine and the Unmanned Systems Command for more details.

items.title: The Coast Guard icebreaker nobody wanted just came back from a 133-day Arctic patrol
items.summary:
Second chances don’t come around too often, but they did for the U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Storis, an icebreaker that started life as a failed towboat for offshore oil rigs but joined America’s maritime security service in 2024–despite one Coast Guard admiral saying at one point that the ship “may, at best, marginally meet our requirements.”

On Saturday, the ship returned to its temporary home port of Seattle after a 133-day, 17,000-nautical-mile deployment where Storis was the only U.S. surface ship in the High Arctic , the region’s northernmost section, according to a Coast Guard press release .

Along the way, the crew carried out the first law enforcement mission by an icebreaker in more than 20 years when they inspected fishing boats in the Bering Sea. They also practiced firing machine guns in extreme cold conditions; escorted a grounded fishing vessel to safety; tested out small drones in extreme cold and at high latitudes; and monitored Chinese-flagged research vessels, which experts say gather oceanographic information for China’s scientific, commercial and military fleets.

items.title: Tehran Widens Attacks On Gulf Nations After Latest U.S. Strike On Iranian Island
items.summary:
Amid stalled efforts to find a diplomatic solution to the conflict between the U.S. and Iran, the Islamic Republic is stepping up attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain, two nations that host American bases. Wednesday’s strikes took place after the latest U.S. attack on Iran’s Qeshm Island .

These actions, along with other developments we will discuss below, raise questions about whether the Middle East could erupt into a new round of intense fighting.

New Iranian Attacks On Gulf Nations 

On Wednesday, Kuwait and Bahrain said they both intercepted Iranian strikes. For Kuwait, it was the first time since September it had been attacked. The strikes on Bahrain marked a continuation of Iranian attacks that began Nov. 13 after they had been paused for two months .

These strikes appear to be an escalation of Iranian actions in response to a U.S. attack on Qeshm Island on Tuesday, The Associated Press suggested . We will discuss that in more detail later in this story.

“Kuwaiti air defenses are currently countering hostile drone attacks,” the Kuwaiti Army posted on X early Wednesday morning local time. “The General Staff of the Army notes that any explosion sounds heard are the result of air defense systems intercepting hostile attacks. Everyone is requested to comply with the security and safety instructions issued by the relevant authorities.”

items.title: Europe Is Exploring Orbital Deep Strike Weapons
items.summary:
Europe is beginning to explore the possibility of delivering conventional military payloads from orbit , with the German arm of defense behemoth MBDA and space transportation company ATMOS Space Cargo teaming up to investigate a concept known as Precision Orbital Deep Strike (PODS). The proposal involves putting military payloads into space before sending them back through the atmosphere when commanded, potentially offering a radically different approach to long-range precision strike.

ATMOS Space Cargo’s Phoenix 1 capsule is seen attached to the upper stage of its Falcon 9 rocket during its mission on April 21, 2025. ATMOS Space Cargo 

The companies announced their cooperation agreement on November 18, establishing a framework for joint feasibility studies and the design, development, and demonstration of the proposed capability. Initial work will examine system architecture, technical feasibility, payload integration, and potential technology demonstrations.

The concept is undoubtedly hugely ambitious. Getting a payload into orbit and returning it to Earth is a very different problem from developing a reliable weapon capable of striking a designated target with precision and at a predictable time. With that in mind, the agreement represents an initial effort to determine whether such a capability is technically and operationally feasible.

items.t: Europe Is Exploring Orbital Deep Strike Weapons

items.title: Flying Stripped-Down F-15 “Silver Eagles” To Their Limits
items.summary:
Driving across the vast flightline at Robins Air Force Base in Georgia, a prominent hangar bears the title “Welcome to Eagle Country.” A row of nearby smaller ‘barn’ hangars each reveals the telltale silhouette of an F-15 inside it, which on closer inspection are a mixture of either immaculate gray-painted or stripped-down bare metal Strike Eagles . The howl of one of the F-15E’s jet-fuel starters is followed by the sound of its engines spooling up. In the front seat, a pilot from the lesser-known 339th Flight Test Squadron based here is taking one of the bare metal jets up for a test flight.

The Warner Robins Air Logistics Complex here has performed program depot maintenance, known as PDM, on F-15s since 1975 and this critical support of the U.S. Air Force’s Eagle fleet continues today. The C-5M Galaxy , C-17 Globemaster , and C-130 Hercules fleets also receive deep maintenance here.

Roughly every seven years an F-15 comes to Warner Robins for PDM in the large Air Logistics Complex hangars, where it gets stripped down to the bare bones. The airframe is thoroughly checked over, the latest upgrades are added, and the jet is repaired where necessary by the hardworking depot maintenance team.

With just two squadrons of F-15C/Ds remaining, that fleet has been managed to retain airframes that don’t require PDM. Therefore, the deep maintenance at Robins is now dedicated to F-15E Strike Eagles, with new F-15EXs set to start cycling through in the next few years.

items.t: Flying Stripped-Down F-15 “Silver Eagles” To Their Limits

items.title: U.S. Air Force’s Containerized Surface-To-Air Missile Program Comes Into Sharper Focus
items.summary:
The U.S. Air Force has awarded a flurry of contracts to support its pursuit of a new, lower-cost anti-air missile, as well as containerized launchers to fire them. The Counter-Air Missile Program (CAMP) is targeting designs that cost no more than $500,000 apiece and can be produced at a rate of at least 1,000 per year. The war with Iran, as well as other conflicts in recent years , has driven home a critical need, in general, to expand the depth and breadth of ground-based options for tackling a wide range of aerial threats . CAMP also aligns with Air Force efforts to expand its organic ground-based air defenses , which it has historically relied on the Army to provide. 

The Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) announced today that it, in partnership with Specter Aerospace, had received a $124 million award from the Air Force to develop an anti-air missile under CAMP. This follows news yesterday from Castelion that it had received two separate CAMP contracts covering work on an interceptor, as well as a launch pod to load them into a containerized launcher. Anduril shared last week that it had also secured a deal to develop a launcher in support of this program.

Castelion released this graphic along with the press release about its new CAMP contracts yesterday. Castelion 

The Air Force first shared details about CAMP, which is focused initially on a surface-to-air capability, last year. The service has said the program could also lead to a new air-to-air missile. items.title: Need range time? The Army now has an online reservation system
items.summary:
The Army wants its new reservation system to reduce the wait for test-range time from more than a year to no more than 30 days. Since it launched in August, according to the commander of Test and Evaluation Command, they’re averaging 33.

Companies wanting to test a weapon can submit a proposal with dates and a preferred range, and within 24 hours, a “concierge” will call back to schedule a time.

“There's a perception that testing takes too long to get onto ranges, and at places like White Sands Missile Range—that's booked out. It may take a while to get on,” Maj. Gen. Pat Gaydon said Tuesday at an AUSA event near Washington, D.C. “But that's not the only range, and I think there's a misperception that that's where everyone needs to go to do their testing.”

The Army has opened up Dugway Proving Ground, Utah; the West Cibola Range at Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona; Camp Grayling, Michigan; Camp Shelby, Mississippi; Camp Atterbury, Indiana; and an international range near Tan-Tan, Morocco, for its quick-turnaround reservation system.

items.title: Major AI platforms generated viable plans for terrorist attacks, GAO finds
items.summary:
Four of the most widely used artificial intelligence platforms generated viable plans for attacks on U.S. critical infrastructure and mass-casualty events during covert government testing, despite safeguards designed to prevent their misuse.

According to a Government Accountability Office report published Wednesday, investigators tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok in spring 2026. They found that all four platforms provided information that could help malicious actors plan and carry out attacks.

In each case, the investigators were able to circumvent the platforms’ safety guardrails by using common safeguard-bypassing techniques.

“We got the nefarious information that we were after. So, in this case, those safeguards didn’t work. And I think that’s the story here,” Kevin Walsh, a director of IT and cybersecurity at GAO, said in a podcast interview published alongside the report.

The platforms generated information for two types of attacks: constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device designed to cause mass casualties, and targeting the electrical grid to cause economic damage. The platforms provided details including specific targets, locations, timing and attack methods.

Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate an attack. GAO investigators then worked with experts to verify that the information could be used to carry out the attacks.

items.title: Senate grills acting Navy secretary on Iran war costs, extended deployments
items.summary:
The White House’s pick to lead the Navy didn’t have clear answers Tuesday when lawmakers pressed him about ballooning Iran war costs, the resulting toll on troops deployed to the region, and the service’s overall readiness during a Senate confirmation hearing. 

Hung Cao, a retired Navy captain who has been the service’s acting secretary since April, said the Iran war was a “strain” on resources, but failed to provide the detailed answers sought by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.

“I do not know the daily cost, ma'am…I know the rough costs, how much it's costing us so far,” he told the Senate Armed Services Committee, later adding that it was around $30 billion after Warren quoted estimates of about $32.5 million a day.

Cao also didn’t have an answer when asked how much damage Iranian strikes had caused to the U.S. Naval Base in Bahrain. “We're still making all the assessments because it's a non-permissive area for us to go.” U.S. troops are still in Bahrain; some came under fire yesterday during Iran’s latest strike on radar facilities there.

items.title: This Is What Submarine HMS Vengeance Looks Like After Its Record-Setting Nuclear Deterrence Patrol
items.summary:
When a Royal Navy Vanguard nuclear ballistic missile submarine finally arrived back at its home port on Sunday , it looked every bit like it had been underway for a reported seven months . Images shared with TWZ show the boat caked in a brownish-green hue, a severe example of “ marine [or bio] fouling .” Dripping rust, missing anechoic tiles and plenty of other wear and tear was visible after spending the better part of a year under water. 

The 15,000-ton HMS Vengeance and its crew of about 140 returned to HM Naval Base Clyde in Scotland after a record-setting nuclear deterrence mission. The patrol was part of Operation Relentless, which “ensures at least one nuclear-powered and armed ballistic missile submarine is at sea at all times, deterring our adversaries and protecting the UK and our NATO allies,” the U.K. government said in a release. “As one submarine returns home, another is already at sea continuing this vital patrol.”

The HMS Vengeance arrived Sunday at HM Naval Base Clyde after a seven-month nuclear deterrence mission. (Michael Deveney) 

As we’ve indicated in the past , each boat has 16 missile tubes for UGM-133 Trident II submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs). However, in practice only eight are filled. When on Operation Relentless patrols, Vanguard boats are able to carry a maximum of 40 warheads, with each Trident missile able to carry multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicles (MIRVs).

items.t: This Is What Submarine HMS Vengeance Looks Like After Its Record-Setting Nuclear Deterrence Patrol

items.title: 43 soldiers signed up to play ‘GTA VI’ in exchange for more service
items.summary:
As gamers prepare for what’s expected to be one of the biggest video game launches in history , dozens of soldiers at Fort Stewart, Georgia are also gearing up for a long weekend in Vice City.

According to the Army, 43 soldiers from the 9 th Brigade Engineer Battalion signed up for its unique reenlistment incentive that gives them a four-day weekend to play the new “Grand Theft Auto VI” when it comes out Thursday in exchange for two to six more years of service. 

“Grand Theft Auto,” one of the most popular video game series of the century , gives players a choose-your-own-adventure experience. In “GTA”’s fictional Vice City, which is roughly modeled after Miami, Florida, players can interact with their surroundings and cause mayhem how they see fit: pull off a bank heist, run a criminal enterprise, play golf or tennis, or go on carjackings.

Two soldiers who signed up for the incentive told Task & Purpose that they’re looking forward to a long weekend off to play for a few hours — not endlessly, they clarified. 

“I’m all campaign. I’m all about the heist,” said Sgt. Jamire Smith, a combat engineer, who signed up for the incentive along with six more years in the Army. “I think I have a good 24 hours to waste on it,” he joked.

items.title: US charges Irishman with destroying a $60 million Air Force C-130 with an axe
items.summary:
An Irishman could go to prison for up to 10 years for allegedly destroying a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard C-130H while it was parked for an en route stop at Shannon Airport in Ireland earlier this year. 

On Tuesday, the U.S. Justice Department announced charges against Daithi O’Corrain, 48, for destroying government property. FBI Assistant Director in Charge James Barnacle Jr. said O’Corrain allegedly spent months researching where to infiltrate the airport, how to break into the C-130, which systems to sabotage, and what tools to do it with.

“This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism,” Barnacle said in a Justice Department press release . 

Sabotage 

On April 11, at about 4:39 a.m. local time, O’Corrain breached the airport’s security perimeter, according to the indictment . He allegedly broke the locking mechanism on the rear crew door of the C-130, located on the side of the fuselage, then barricaded himself inside and covered all the windows, except the cockpit windows, using the flight crew’s hammocks.

“O’Corrain attached straps, brackets, and screws to various fixed parts of the aircraft’s interior in order to secure the aircraft’s doors; he also placed ball bearings mixed with epoxy into the aircraft’s door tracks in order to prevent the doors from opening and closing,” the indictment read.

items.title: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck
items.summary:
A group of eight trainee parachutists did the jump, and not far from the ground, disaster struck. Rob Bugden describes how he rebuilt his life after the accident that changed everything

The skydive was going to plan. At 12,000ft, Rob Bugden jumped from the plane, quickly getting himself stable by arching his back to create a solid base. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. And I’m waking up in a hospital in Phoenix.”

It was 21 January 2016, the final day of his Royal Air Force high altitude training in the US, when 30-year-old Bugden collided – mid-air – with his friend, Brook Stebbings. They were moving into the landing stack formation, a vertical queue of eight parachutists flying in a holding pattern at different altitudes, when, at approximately 1,000ft, Stebbings’ knee crashed into him, breaking his neck. They fell to the sand in the middle of the desert, entangled – looking, according to the team on the ground, “like we had a bag of washing above our heads”.
